title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
summary: How rain soaks into the ground to fill aquifers, what the water table is, how wells and pumps reach this hidden water, and why people must use it carefully.
poll: Protecting hidden water underground is just as important as saving water we can see.

versions.title: Water Hiding in the Ground
versions.text:
Can water hide? Yes! It can hide in the ground.

Rain falls down. Some of it soaks in. It goes into the soil. This hidden water is called groundwater.

Soil has small holes. Rock has holes too. Water can fill them up.

Go deep down. All the holes are full. No air is left. This spot has a name. It is the water table.

People dig a hole. It is a well. The well goes past the water table. Water fills it up.

Rain makes the water rise. A dry time makes it drop. Then a well can go dry.

Farmers pump the water. They grow crops with it. Towns pump it too. We drink it and wash with it.

Rain is rare here. So we must care for this hidden water. We do not want it to run out.

versions.title: Finding Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain falls on the land. Where does it go? Some of it soaks into the soil.

Soil is not solid. It has lots of tiny holes. Rock has tiny holes too. Water seeps down. It fills up these small spaces. This hidden water is called groundwater.

Go down far enough. Every hole is full of water. No air is left at all. The top of this wet part has a name. It is the water table.

To get this water, people dig a well. A well is a deep hole. It goes down past the water table. Water fills the bottom of the well.

After rain, the water table rises up. In a long dry time, it sinks down. If it sinks too far, a well can run dry.

Farmers pump water from wells to grow crops. Towns pump water too. People drink it, cook with it, and wash with it.

Rain falls rarely here in Saudi Arabia. So people care for this hidden water. No one wants a well to run dry.

Farmers pump water from wells to water their crops. Towns and cities pump groundwater too, so families have water to drink, cook with, and wash.

versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain falls on the land. Where does it go? Much of it soaks down into the soil, out of sight.

Soil is almost never solid all the way through. It is full of tiny holes and narrow cracks, too small to see. Rock has tiny holes too. As rainwater seeps down, it fills these small spaces. This hidden water, stored inside the ground, is called groundwater.

Dig deep enough, and you reach a point where every hole is already full of water. No air is left at all. The upper edge of this soaked layer has its own name. It is called the water table.

To reach groundwater, people dig or drill a well, a deep hole that reaches down past the water table. Once the well goes deep enough, water slowly fills its bottom.

After heavy rain, the water table tends to rise closer to the surface. During a long dry season, it slowly sinks lower instead. If it sinks too far down, a well that once worked can run completely dry.

Farmers pump water from wells to water their crops across dry fields. Towns and cities pump groundwater too, so families always have water to drink, cook with, and wash.

Rain falls so rarely across much of Saudi Arabia that people must take great care of this hidden water. Nobody wants a well that a whole village depends on to run dry.

versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain falls on the land. Much of it does not stay on the surface for long. It soaks down into the soil, out of sight.

Soil and rock are almost never completely solid. They are full of tiny holes and cracks, too small to notice. These materials are permeable, meaning water can pass through them. Rainwater seeps down and fills these tiny spaces. This hidden water is called groundwater.

Dig deep enough, and you reach a zone where every hole is already saturated, meaning it is full of water with no air left. The upper edge of this saturated zone has a name. It is the water table.

The layer of rock or sand that holds groundwater is called an aquifer. It lets water flow through it. Some aquifers are huge. Some took thousands of years to fill.

To reach groundwater, people dig or drill a well. It is a deep hole that reaches past the water table into the aquifer below. Pumps then pump the water up to the surface.

After heavy rain, water helps recharge the aquifer. This raises the water table. In a long dry season, the water table sinks instead, and a well can run dry.

Farmers pump groundwater to water their crops. Towns and cities pump it too, so families have water to drink, cook with, and wash. Rain falls so rarely in Saudi Arabia that people must manage this hidden water with care.

versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain falls across the land. Much of it does not remain on the surface for long. It gradually infiltrates the soil, disappearing from view within hours or days as the storm passes.

Soil and rock are almost never entirely solid. They are riddled with tiny pores and cracks, far too small for the eye to notice without equipment. These porous materials allow water to pass through them fairly easily, a quality called permeability. Rainwater gradually seeps downward and fills these tiny spaces, one layer at a time. This hidden water is known as groundwater, and it exists almost everywhere beneath our feet, even beneath deserts that look dry on the surface.

Travel deep enough, and you reach a zone where every pore is already saturated, meaning it is completely filled with water and no air remains. The upper boundary of this saturated zone has a name: the water table, a boundary that rises or falls across a region, depending on rainfall and geology.

The layer of rock or sand that holds groundwater is called an aquifer. It lets water flow through with relative ease. Some aquifers extend for miles underground, and several ancient ones beneath the Arabian Peninsula took thousands of years to fill with rain, water scientists call fossil water because of its great age.

To reach groundwater, people dig or drill a well, a deep shaft that descends past the water table into the aquifer below. Pumps then accomplish the extraction of water, drawing it up to the surface for drinking, cooking, and farming.

After heavy rain, water infiltrates downward and helps recharge the aquifer, raising the water table closer to the surface. During a long dry season, the water table sinks lower instead, and a well can eventually run dry, forcing communities to drill deeper wells.

Farmers extract groundwater to water their fields, while towns and cities draw it so families have water to drink, cook with, and wash. Because rain is rare across Saudi Arabia, and some aquifers recharge slowly, hydrologists now monitor water tables closely, hoping to prevent the depletion of aquifers a region depends on, and to keep this hidden water sustainable for future generations.

versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain falls across a landscape. Much of it does not linger on the surface for long. It gradually permeates the soil, vanishing from view within hours or days as the storm moves on.

Soil and rock are almost never entirely solid. They are riddled with microscopic pores and narrow fractures, far too small for the unaided eye to detect. These porous materials allow water to pass through with relative ease, a property called permeability. Rainwater steadily seeps downward and fills these minute spaces, layer by layer. This hidden water, stored within the subsurface, is known as groundwater, and it exists almost everywhere beneath our feet, even beneath deserts that appear utterly dry at the surface.

Descend deep enough, and you encounter a zone where every pore is already saturated, meaning it is entirely filled with water and no air remains. The upper boundary of this saturated zone carries a specific name: the water table, a boundary that rarely stays level, rising or falling across a region depending on rainfall and geology.

The rock or sand layer that stores groundwater is termed an aquifer. It permits water to flow through with relative freedom. Certain aquifers extend for hundreds of miles underground, and several ancient ones beneath the Arabian Peninsula required thousands of years to fill, water hydrologists sometimes label fossil water because of its remarkable age.

To access this groundwater, people excavate or drill a well, a deep shaft descending past the water table into the aquifer beneath. Pumps then accomplish the extraction of this water, hoisting it to the surface for drinking, cooking, and farming.

Following heavy rainfall, water permeates downward and helps recharge the aquifer, raising the water table closer to the surface. During a prolonged dry season, the water table descends instead, and a well that once functioned dependably can run entirely dry, compelling communities to drill ever deeper wells.

Farmers extract groundwater to irrigate their fields, while towns and cities draw upon it so families have water for drinking, cooking, and washing. Because rainfall is infrequent across much of Saudi Arabia, and certain aquifers recharge with extreme slowness, hydrologists now monitor water tables with rigor, striving to forestall the depletion of aquifers entire regions depend on, and to preserve this hidden resource as a sustainable asset for generations to come.

These porous materials allow water to pass through with relative ease, a property geologists call permeability. Rainwater steadily seeps downward and fills these minute spaces, layer by layer, much as a sponge absorbs a spilled liquid. To access this groundwater, people excavate or drill a well, a deep shaft that descends past the water table into the aquifer beneath. Pumps then accomplish the extraction of this water, hoisting it toward the surface for drinking, cooking, and farming.

Following substantial rainfall, water permeates downward and helps recharge the aquifer, raising the water table closer to the surface. versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Precipitation falls across a landscape. Much of it does not linger on the surface for long. It gradually permeates the soil, vanishing from view within hours or days as the storm system moves elsewhere, leaving the ground looking deceptively dry once more.

Soil and rock, it turns out, are almost never entirely solid. They are riddled with microscopic pores and narrow fractures, far too small for the unaided eye to detect without magnification. These porous materials allow water to pass through with relative ease, a property geologists call permeability. Rainwater steadily seeps downward and fills these minute spaces, layer by layer, much as a sponge absorbs a spilled liquid until it can hold no more. This hidden reserve of water is known as groundwater, and it exists almost everywhere beneath our feet, even beneath deserts that appear utterly dry at the surface.

Descend deep enough, and one encounters a zone where every pore and fracture is already saturated, meaning it is entirely filled with water and no air remains whatsoever. The upper boundary of this saturated zone carries a specific name: the water table, a boundary that rarely stays level, rising or falling gradually across a region depending on rainfall patterns and the underlying geology.

The rock or sand layer that stores groundwater and permits it to flow through with relative freedom is termed an aquifer. Certain aquifers extend for hundreds of miles underground, and several ancient ones beneath the Arabian Peninsula required thousands of years to fill with rainwater that fell long before recorded history, water hydrologists label fossil water because of its remarkable age, far older than any civilization.

To access this groundwater, people excavate or drill a well, a deep shaft that descends past the water table and penetrates into the aquifer beneath. Pumps then accomplish the extraction of this water, hoisting it toward the surface for drinking, cooking, and agriculture throughout the Kingdom.

Following substantial rainfall, water gradually permeates downward and helps recharge the aquifer, raising the water table closer to the surface. During a prolonged dry season, or whenever extraction exceeds natural recharge, the water table descends instead, and a well that once functioned dependably can eventually run entirely dry, compelling communities to drill ever deeper wells that cost more each time.

Farmers extract groundwater to irrigate their fields across wide agricultural regions, while towns and cities draw upon it so families consistently have water for drinking, cooking, and washing every day. Because rainfall is infrequent across much of Saudi Arabia, and certain fossil aquifers recharge with extreme slowness over centuries, hydrologists now monitor water tables with increasing rigor, striving to forestall the irreversible depletion of aquifers that entire regions depend on, and to preserve this hidden resource as a genuinely sustainable asset for generations yet to come.

versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain that falls across a landscape rarely remains at the surface for long; most of it steadily permeates the soil and the rock beneath, vanishing from view within hours as it moves into a vast, hidden network of pores and fractures too small for the human eye to perceive without magnification. Because these materials are porous and permeable, water seeps downward through them much as it would through a sponge, gradually accumulating in a reservoir that geologists call groundwater, a resource that exists almost everywhere beneath the surface, even beneath landscapes that appear, from above, to be entirely arid.

At a certain depth, every available pore and fracture becomes saturated, meaning water fills the rock completely and no air remains trapped within it. The upper boundary of this saturated zone is known as the water table, an irregular surface that rises and falls across a region in response to rainfall, underlying geology, and the rate at which people extract water from it. The particular rock or sand formation capable of storing and transmitting this water efficiently is called an aquifer, and certain aquifers beneath the Arabian Peninsula are extraordinarily ancient, having accumulated their water, often termed fossil water, over many thousands of years, long before recorded history began.

To draw upon this hidden resource, people drill wells that descend past the water table directly into the aquifer below, employing powerful pumps to accomplish the extraction of water that would otherwise remain inaccessible. Sustained rainfall gradually recharges an aquifer, raising the water table nearer the surface, whereas prolonged drought, or extraction that outpaces recharge, causes the water table to decline, occasionally rendering once-reliable wells entirely dry and forcing communities to drill ever deeper at considerable expense.

Agricultural operations depend heavily upon pumped groundwater to irrigate crops across regions where rainfall alone could never sustain farming, while municipal water systems rely on wells to supply households throughout the Kingdom with water for drinking, cooking, and washing. Because many of the Arabian Peninsula's aquifers recharge extraordinarily slowly, hydrologists and policymakers now monitor water tables with considerable rigor, tracking subtle changes over months and years in an effort to detect depletion before it becomes irreversible.

This ongoing vigilance reflects a broader recognition that groundwater, however invisible, is a genuinely finite resource in an arid region, one that must be managed sustainably if future generations are to inherit wells that still yield water rather than empty, depleted shafts. Scientists continue refining their estimates of how quickly particular aquifers can safely be drawn upon without threatening long-term supply, work that directly shapes decisions about where new farms, cities, and wells may reasonably be established across the Kingdom, and that will likely matter even more as populations and farms continue to grow.

versions.title: The Water Table: Hidden Water Underground
versions.text:
Rain that falls across a landscape seldom remains at the surface for long; the overwhelming majority of it steadily permeates the soil and the underlying rock, vanishing from view within hours as it migrates into a vast, hidden network of microscopic pores and fractures far too small for the unaided human eye to perceive without magnification. Because these subsurface materials are porous and permeable, water seeps downward through them in much the way it would through an ordinary sponge, gradually accumulating within a reservoir that geologists term groundwater, a resource that exists almost ubiquitously beneath the surface, even beneath landscapes that appear, when viewed from above, to be entirely and permanently arid.

At a sufficient depth, every available pore and fracture becomes fully saturated, meaning that water fills the surrounding rock completely and no air whatsoever remains trapped within its structure. The upper boundary of this saturated zone is formally designated the water table, an irregular and constantly shifting surface that rises and falls across a given region in direct response to rainfall patterns, underlying geology, and, increasingly, the rate at which human communities extract water from it. The particular rock or sand formation capable of storing and transmitting this water with reasonable efficiency is termed an aquifer, and several aquifers beneath the Arabian Peninsula are extraordinarily ancient, having accumulated their contents, frequently described as fossil water, over many thousands of years, long antedating recorded human history.

To draw upon this largely invisible resource, people drill wells that descend past the water table and directly into the aquifer beneath, employing substantial pumps to accomplish the extraction of water that would otherwise remain wholly inaccessible to human use. Sustained rainfall gradually recharges a given aquifer, incrementally raising its associated water table nearer the surface, whereas prolonged drought, or extraction that significantly outpaces natural recharge, causes the water table to decline steadily, occasionally rendering once-dependable wells entirely dry and compelling communities to drill ever deeper at considerable and mounting expense.

Agricultural operations throughout the region depend heavily upon pumped groundwater to irrigate crops in areas where rainfall alone could never sustain meaningful farming, while municipal water systems rely extensively upon wells to supply households throughout the Kingdom with water intended for drinking, cooking, and washing alike. Because numerous aquifers across the Arabian Peninsula recharge with extraordinary slowness, hydrologists and policymakers alike now monitor water tables with considerable methodological rigor, meticulously tracking subtle fluctuations over months and years in a sustained effort to detect incipient depletion well before it becomes practically irreversible.

This ongoing vigilance reflects a broader, increasingly urgent recognition that groundwater, however invisible to ordinary observation, constitutes a genuinely finite resource in an arid region, one that must be managed sustainably if future generations are to inherit productive wells rather than empty, thoroughly depleted shafts. Scientists continue refining their quantitative estimates of precisely how much water particular aquifers can safely yield without jeopardizing long-term supply, research that directly and substantially informs decisions about where new farms, new cities, and new wells may reasonably be established across the Kingdom in the decades ahead.

wrong.C: Aquifers are already made of rock or sand; they do not turn to stone.
wrong.D: Recharge happens slowly, not instantly.

questions.stem: Some aquifers beneath Saudi Arabia took thousands of years to fill. What does this suggest about using that water quickly?
options: It is harmless, since the water refills in just days
It makes no real difference how much water is pumped
Each year's new rain instantly replaces all of the water
It could run out and not be replaced for a long time
questions.why: Because these aquifers took so long to fill, pumping them quickly could use up water that will not be replaced for ages.

wrong.A: The article says recharge can take thousands of years, not days.
wrong.B: How much is pumped matters a great deal for a slow-recharging aquifer.
wrong.C: Rain cannot instantly replace water that took thousands of years to collect.

questions.stem: A well suddenly produces no water after a long drought. What most likely happened?
options: The water table sank below the well's bottom
The surrounding aquifer slowly became permeable
An unusual amount of rain recharged the aquifer
The well was dug into solid rock with no holes
questions.why: During a long dry season, the water table sinks, and if it drops below the bottom of the well, the well runs dry.

wrong.B: Aquifers are already permeable; drought does not change that.
wrong.C: The problem described is a drought, so there was too little rain, not too much.
wrong.D: Wells reach down into permeable rock or sand, not solid rock with no holes.

questions.stem: Read: "Because these materials are permeable, meaning water can pass through them." What does permeable mean?
options: Completely solid with no holes at all
Extremely hot underground
Able to let water pass through easily
Full of salt and minerals
questions.why: The sentence explains that permeable materials let water pass through them.

wrong.A: Permeable materials have tiny openings, not solid walls.
wrong.B: Heat is not part of this definition.
wrong.D: Salt and minerals are not mentioned here.

questions.stem: How does the author help readers understand how an aquifer fills with water over time?
options: By listing exact dates of several famous past droughts and floods in the area
By walking through, in order, how rain soaks in and slowly recharges it
By telling a long story about one family's old well in a village
By describing the steps of a science experiment in a school lab
questions.why: The author walks through the process in order: rain soaks in, fills the tiny spaces, and recharges the aquifer over time.

wrong.A: No dates of droughts are listed.
wrong.C: No single family's story is told.
wrong.D: No lab experiment is described.

MID.prompt: Explain how an aquifer gets its water and how people reach it, using at least three steps in order.
checklist: I explained at least three steps in order.
I used words from the article such as aquifer, saturated, and recharge.
I used order words like first, then, and finally.
MID.modelAnswer: First, rain soaks down through permeable soil and rock. Then, the water fills tiny holes and cracks until that layer becomes saturated, and the layer that holds and lets this water flow through is called an aquifer. Finally, people drill a well down past the water table into the aquifer and pump the water up to use for drinking, cooking, and farming.

keyWords.definition: full of tiny holes or spaces that can hold or let through liquid
keyWords.example: Porous volcanic rock can soak up rainwater like a sponge.

keyWords.definition: the act of removing or drawing something out, often from the ground
keyWords.example: The extraction of oil requires drilling deep beneath the surface.

keyWords.definition: a serious reduction in supply caused by using something faster than it is replaced
keyWords.example: Years of heavy fishing led to the depletion of fish in the bay.

keyWords.definition: to carefully watch or measure something over a period of time
keyWords.example: Doctors monitor a patient's heartbeat throughout the night.

keyWords.definition: able to continue for a long time without running out or causing harm
keyWords.example: The farm switched to sustainable methods that protect the soil for future harvests.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Hydrologists monitor water tables so pumped aquifers stay sustainable
Wells only work properly during years of unusually heavy rainfall
Fossil water is a rare type of water found only inside fossils
Saudi Arabia receives more yearly rainfall than any other nation
questions.why: The article explains how groundwater fills porous aquifers, how wells extract it, and why monitoring helps keep the resource sustainable.

wrong.B: Wells draw on groundwater that built up over time, not only on fresh rainfall.
wrong.C: Fossil water refers to very old groundwater, not water found in fossils.
wrong.D: The article says rain is rare across much of Saudi Arabia.

questions.stem: Read: "a zone where every pore and fracture is already saturated... porous materials allow water to pass through." What does porous mean?
options: Extremely heavy and dense throughout
Full of tiny holes that let liquid through
Resistant to any kind of water at all
Found only deep inside solid, unbroken rock
questions.why: Porous materials contain tiny holes that allow water to pass through and be stored within them.

wrong.A: Density is not what the word describes.
wrong.C: Porous materials let water through, rather than resisting it.
wrong.D: Porous materials can be rock or sand near or far from the surface.

questions.stem: What does extraction mean in this article?
options: Pumping or drawing water out of the ground
Letting rain soak naturally into the soil
Measuring the depth of a well with a rope
Building a new well by hand
questions.why: The article uses extraction to describe pumps drawing water up out of the ground.

wrong.B: Rain soaking in is called recharge, the opposite process.
wrong.C: Measuring with a rope is not described in the article.
wrong.D: Building a well is a separate step from extracting water.

questions.stem: What is fossil water?
options: Water found trapped inside the bones of ancient animals
Fresh rainwater that fell sometime within the last few months
Ancient groundwater that took thousands of years to build up
Water that is pumped directly out of the open sea
questions.why: The article describes fossil water as ancient groundwater that took many thousands of years to fill an aquifer.

wrong.A: Fossil water is not described as being inside animal bones.
wrong.B: Fossil water is described as extremely old, not recent.
wrong.D: Fossil water comes from underground aquifers, not the sea.

questions.stem: What happens when extraction of groundwater exceeds the rate of recharge?
options: The water table rises and the well overflows with water, so the farmers have more
The aquifer instantly refills from the sea, so it never goes dry
Nothing changes, since groundwater is unlimited and never runs out
The water table falls, and the aquifer can become depleted
questions.why: When people pump out more water than recharge replaces, the water table falls and the aquifer can become depleted.

wrong.A: Too much extraction lowers the water table rather than raising it.
wrong.B: Aquifers are not described as connected to the sea.
wrong.C: The article treats groundwater as a limited resource, not an unlimited one.

questions.stem: A hydrologist observes a water table steadily dropping for many years. What can be concluded?
options: The region has had unusually heavy rainfall for many years
More water is being extracted than is being recharged
The aquifer has become completely saturated with water
The well has stopped being used altogether by the town
questions.why: A steadily dropping water table over many years points to extraction outpacing recharge.

wrong.A: Heavy rainfall would tend to raise, not lower, the water table.
wrong.C: A fully saturated aquifer would not show a steadily falling water table.
wrong.D: An unused well would not, by itself, explain a region's dropping water table.

questions.stem: Why might a region favor sustainable management of its aquifers over unlimited pumping?
options: Because many aquifers recharge slowly and could become depleted
Because unlimited pumping is said to always increase rainfall
Because sustainable management makes every well deeper automatically
Because aquifers are known to recharge within a single season
questions.why: Because some aquifers take thousands of years to recharge, pumping without limits risks permanent depletion.

wrong.B: Pumping groundwater does not affect rainfall.
wrong.C: Management practices do not automatically change well depth.
wrong.D: The article says some aquifers take thousands of years to recharge, not a single season.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention that hydrologists now monitor water tables with increasing rigor?
options: To argue that careful monitoring makes aquifers recharge faster
To show that tracking helps prevent irreversible depletion
To compare two completely unrelated kinds of pumps
To describe in detail how wells are originally drilled
questions.why: Mentioning careful monitoring shows why tracking water tables matters for preventing permanent depletion.

wrong.A: Monitoring tracks recharge; it does not speed it up.
wrong.C: No comparison of different pump types is made.
wrong.D: Well drilling is explained elsewhere, not as the point of this detail.

HIGH.prompt: Should regions limit how much groundwater they pump each year? Support your opinion with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence connects to my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think regions should limit how much groundwater they pump each year. The article explains that some aquifers beneath the Arabian Peninsula took thousands of years to fill with fossil water, so pumping it out quickly could cause depletion that cannot be reversed for a very long time. Because extraction that outpaces recharge causes the water table to fall, monitoring and limiting pumping helps keep this hidden resource sustainable for future generations.

options: They grow crops with it
They sail boats on it
They build roads with it
They turn it into rain
LOW.why: The text says farmers pump the water and grow crops with it.

wrong.B: The text does not say farmers sail boats.
wrong.C: The text does not say roads are built with it.
wrong.D: Farmers cannot turn water into rain.

LOW.stem: The text says farmers pump the water. What does pump mean?
options: push water down deeper
make water stand still
pull water up and out
turn water into ice
LOW.why: Farmers and towns use the water, so pumping brings it up out of the ground.

wrong.A: People want to use the water, so they bring it up, not down.
wrong.B: Pumping moves water; it does not hold it still.
wrong.D: The text says nothing about ice.

LOW.stem: What is true of the holes at the water table?
options: They are all full of air
They are all full of water
They are all full of sand
They are all empty
LOW.why: The text says all the holes are full and no air is left at the water table.

wrong.A: The text says no air is left.
wrong.C: The holes are filled with water, not sand.
wrong.D: The text says the holes are full.

LOW.stem: Towns pump more water than rain brings back. What will probably happen?
options: The water table will go up
The wells will fill up fast
The rain will fall more often
The water table will go down
LOW.why: The text says rain makes the water rise and a dry time makes it drop, so taking out more water than comes back lowers it.

wrong.A: More water leaves than comes back, so it will not rise.
wrong.B: Wells would run low, not fill up.
wrong.C: Pumping water does not change how often it rains.

MID.stem: How does water from a well reach the surface?
options: Rain pushes it up
Wind blows it up
Pumps lift it up
Soil squeezes it out
MID.why: The text says pumps pump the water up to the surface.

wrong.A: The text does not say rain pushes it up.
wrong.B: The text does not say wind brings water up.
wrong.D: The text does not say soil squeezes water out.

MID.stem: In the text, what does the word recharge mean?
options: dig deeper
fill up again
dry out
clean off
MID.why: Heavy rain adds water to the aquifer and raises the water table, so recharge means to fill again.

wrong.A: Rain does not dig anything.
wrong.C: Rain adds water, so the aquifer does not dry out.
wrong.D: The text does not say the aquifer is cleaned.

MID.stem: What does heavy rain do to the water table?
options: It lowers the water table
It dries up the wells
It turns soil to rock
It raises the water table
MID.why: The text says after heavy rain the aquifer is recharged, which raises the water table.

wrong.A: The water table goes down in a dry season, not after heavy rain.
wrong.B: Wells run dry in a long dry season.
wrong.C: The text does not say rain turns soil to rock.

MID.stem: Why does the author begin by describing rain falling on the land?
options: To show where groundwater comes from
To warn people about floods in towns
To explain how a well is dug
To compare farms with big cities
MID.why: The article starts with rain soaking into the soil, which becomes groundwater.

wrong.B: Floods are not the topic of the opening.
wrong.C: Wells are explained in a later paragraph.
wrong.D: The opening does not compare farms and cities.

HIGH.stem: According to the article, where does groundwater exist?
options: Only beneath very rainy forests
Only under the largest rivers
Only beneath farmers' fields
Almost everywhere underground
HIGH.why: The text says groundwater exists almost everywhere beneath our feet, even beneath deserts.

wrong.A: The text says it also exists beneath deserts.
wrong.B: The text does not limit groundwater to places under rivers.
wrong.C: The text does not limit groundwater to farm fields.

HIGH.stem: In the text, what does the word recharge mean?
options: to empty out slowly
to fill up again
to heat up again
to clean off dirt
HIGH.why: After heavy rain, water moves down into the aquifer and raises the water table, so it is filled again.

wrong.A: Rain adds water, so it does not empty the aquifer.
wrong.C: The text does not talk about heat.
wrong.D: The text does not talk about cleaning.

HIGH.stem: How does heavy rain affect the water table?
options: It lowers it, so wells go dry
It keeps it exactly the same
It raises it nearer the surface
It turns it into fossil water
HIGH.why: The text says rain recharges the aquifer and raises the water table closer to the surface.

wrong.A: Wells run dry in a long dry season, not after heavy rain.
wrong.B: The text says the water table rises or falls with rainfall.
wrong.D: Fossil water is very old water that took thousands of years to fill an aquifer.

HIGH.stem: Why might communities drill deeper wells in a long dry season?
options: The water table sinks lower
The rain fills the aquifer
Farmers need less water
The wells get wider
HIGH.why: The text says the water table sinks in a long dry season and a well can run dry, so wells must reach lower.

wrong.B: The aquifer is not filled in a dry season.
wrong.C: The text does not say farmers need less water.
wrong.D: The text does not say wells get wider.
